readings.title: 速度的暴政
readings.text: We tend to assume that whatever saves time must improve life, and the whole machinery of modern innovation rests upon this assumption. Yet the evidence deserves closer scrutiny. When letters took weeks, a reply meant days of reflection; when messages arrive in seconds, replies arrive in reflex. The faster the exchange, the thinner the thought inside it. Defenders of speed argue that quick communication merely removes dead waiting-time, leaving thinking untouched — a plausible claim, but an empirically doubtful one: studies of workplace messaging suggest the opposite, that pace sets depth rather than serving it. The real implication is uncomfortable. If thought expands to fill available time, then every technology that shrinks time shrinks thought also. This is not an argument for returning to quills and sailing ships; inevitability is not the question. The question is whether we will cultivate deliberate slowness on purpose, in some corners of life, precisely because the rest of life accelerates beyond our control. Speed is a magnificent servant. As a master, it quietly starves whatever it feeds on.

questions.q: What assumption does the author challenge?
What do workplace-messaging studies suggest?
What solution does the author propose?
options: Deliberately keep some corners of life slow

readings.title: 选择的幻觉
readings.text: Supermarkets stock forty kinds of jam and call it freedom; economists long treated this equation as obvious. A curious paradox, however, has emerged from decades of consumer research: beyond a certain point, added options paralyse rather than liberate. Faced with twenty-four varieties, shoppers buy less; faced with six, they buy more and regret less. The prevailing defence of unlimited choice — that individuals know their own preferences best — quietly contradicts how preference actually forms. We discover what we want largely by choosing, comparing and, crucially, by living with results; a catalogue of infinite alternatives makes every chosen life look like a failed experiment. Critics reply that restricting choice patronises the public, and where choice is arbitrary, they are right. But no one advocates removing varieties of bread. The serious argument concerns defaults: pension plans, medical consents, news feeds. Whoever designs the default designs the outcome, and there the vocabulary of freedom has been borrowed by engineering. A mature society would stop counting options and start auditing them — asking not 'how many?' but 'chosen how, and by whom?'

questions.q: What does consumer research show?
options: Beyond a point extra options paralyse buyers

questions.q: Why does endless comparison harm satisfaction?
options: It makes every chosen life feel like a failed experiment

questions.q: Where should society focus according to the author?
options: On auditing how defaults are designed

readings.title: 注意力的经济学
readings.text: Herbert Simon observed that wealth of information creates poverty of attention, and half a century later his aside reads like prophecy. The services we call free are paid for in exactly that coinage: minutes, mornings, and the capacity for sustained thought. Advertisers once rented attention briefly; platforms now farm it industrially, harvesting engagement with machines tuned — by empirical experiment, not accident — to provoke indignation, envy, and compulsive return. It would be comfortable to dismiss such design as harmless entertainment, but scarcity imposes discipline: whatever consumes attention consumes the raw material of citizenship, craftsmanship, and love. Some conclude that regulation alone can restore balance, treating attention as utilities treat water; others place faith in individual discipline, an answer that flatters the will and ignores the laboratory. Both positions share a mistake — treating attention as a private resource. It is also a shared one, like air in a theatre: when everyone stands, no one sees better. The justification for collective norms, from school phone bans to quiet carriages, is simply this. Attention is cultivated socially or it is not cultivated at all.

questions.q: How are 'free' services really paid for?
options: With users' time and sustained thought

questions.q: What mistake do both regulatory and personal-discipline answers share?
options: They treat attention as purely private

questions.q: What is the author's conclusion?

readings.title: 机器与手艺
readings.text: Every generation believes its machines finally abolish skill, and every generation is wrong in an instructive way. The loom did not end weaving; it moved judgement upstream, into pattern and thread. Mechanization removed muscle work; automation now removes routine decisions, and again the fear is of endings while the reality is relocation — of where human judgement sits inside the work. What genuinely disappears in this migration is not skill but visibility. When a carpenter planes a board, quality is public: the hand corrects the eye corrects the hand, and error teaches instantly. When software completes our sentences and cameras complete our photographs, correction still occurs, but silently, elsewhere, by systems whose standards we did not set and cannot inspect. The result is competence without apprenticeship. This suggests a principle for education in an automated age: teach judgement where the machines are weakest — framing problems, weighing values, noticing when a plausible answer is wrong — and treat fluency with tools as necessary but shallow. Machines inherit our routines. Only we can discern which routines deserved inheriting.

questions.q: What actually disappears with automation, says the author?
options: The visibility of skill and correction

questions.q: What should education emphasise?
What line ends the essay?
options: Machines inherit routines; we must judge which deserve it

readings.title: 城市的孤独
readings.text: Eight million neighbours, the saying goes, and not one to borrow salt from. Urban loneliness is usually described as a modern failure, yet the phenomenon is older than elevators: crowd density and neighbourliness have always traded against each other. What is genuinely new is not isolation but its justification. Previous generations experienced city anonymity as loss; we have begun to sell it as liberation — freedom from the village eye, the borrowed ladder, the obligation to attend. There is truth in that freedom, and critics who romanticise communal villages ignore their surveillance and their suffocation. But marketing anonymity as pure gain distorts the ledger. Sociological evidence is fairly consistent: moderate, low-stakes neighbourhood contact measurably protects mental health, while total anonymity corrodes it. The sensible position therefore refuses both nostalgia and triumphalism. Cities need what might be engineered smallness: courtyards over towers, corner shops over chains, third places over private screens — designs that make casual acquaintance cheap and refusal optional. Loneliness is not the price of liberty. Bad architecture is. Liberty, like a garden, needs walls in the right places, and gates.

questions.q: What is genuinely new about urban loneliness?
What do critics of village-life romanticism point out?
options: Villages offered surveillance and suffocation too

questions.q: What does 'bad architecture' mean here?
options: Tall towers and chains that prevent casual contact

readings.title: 语言在退化吗？
readings.text: Every civilisation complains that its language is rotting, and every complaint is eventually embarrassed by the dictionary. Latin parents scolded late-Latin slang; eighteenth-century essayists feared the novel would ruin English prose; my own schooling deplored 'hopefully' as a sentence adverb. Language survived us all. Yet the familiar rebuttal — that change equals life — can become its own superficial slogan, excusing every sloppiness as vitality. A subtler position distinguishes change in convention from decay in precision. When pronunciation drifts, only pedants object; when the shared vocabulary for describing feeling thins, something real is lost, for words are instruments of thought, and blunt instruments cut rough outlines. The honest argument, then, is not whether language changes — it must — but which changes we resist and which we adopt. That is a collective decision, made story by story and classroom by classroom. Languages do not die of natural causes; they die of disuse in particular registers by particular communities. Decay is not destiny. It is a budget, and every generation votes on it, mostly by accident.

vocab.dEn: style of language for a context

questions.q: What flaw does the author find in 'change equals life'?
options: It can excuse every sloppiness as vitality

questions.q: What distinction does the author draw?
options: Change in convention vs decay in precision

questions.q: How do languages actually die?
options: Disuse in specific registers by specific communities

readings.title: 进步的两张面孔
readings.text: Ask whether the century improved, and averages answer yes while kitchens answer more quietly. National income climbed; so, less famously, did the distance between the climb and those who carried it. Economic historians call this distribution; families call it Tuesday. The intellectual difficulty is that both faces are real. Prosperity is genuine — medicine, mobility, and full stomachs are not metaphors — and yet aggregate growth can proceed for decades while inequality quietly re-prices the basics: housing, healthcare, security — goods whose supply cannot expand as easily as desires. Defenders of growth reply that redistribution, not production, is the problem; critics reply that production has captured redistribution, which is why every reform arrives means-tested, stigmatised, and late. Between them lies a simpler test that citizens might apply to any decade's report card: did a person of average luck find life becoming more navigable? Not richer — navigable. By that criterion, progress is neither myth nor machine; it is a direction, reversible, chosen policy by policy. The twentieth century proves we can move that way. The present one is deciding whether we remember how.

questions.q: What does 'families call it Tuesday' suggest?
options: Growth feels abstract in daily life

questions.q: Why can growth coexist with hardship?
options: Basics like housing get re-priced by inequality

questions.q: What simple test does the author propose for progress?
options: Whether average-luck lives become more navigable

readings.title: 论无聊的价值
readings.text: Boredom has acquired the reputation of a disease, and we carry the cure permanently in our pockets. Waiting rooms, queues, elevators — every gap is now filled before it can be felt. The assumption that boredom is mere discomfort deserves challenge, because biographically it seems closer to a workshop. Nearly everyone can recall that ideas arrive not during effort but in the vacancy after it: walks, showers, trains. Psychologists explain this as consolidation; older traditions called it incubation; either way, the mechanism requires empty time, and empty time is precisely what the feed abolishes. The objection is immediate — that romanticising boredom romanticises privilege, since the poor have endured enforced idleness for centuries. It is a fair hit, and it sharpens the proposal rather than defeating it: what matters is chosen emptiness, the difference between a fallow field and abandoned one. To cultivate boredom, then, is a discipline of the leisured mind, not a luxury good: ten minutes of nothing between tasks, one walk without headphones, a child permitted to be boring on a Sunday afternoon. Minds, like fields, produce nothing forever unless left occasionally unplanted.

questions.q: According to the essay, when do ideas typically arrive?
What is the strong objection the author concedes?
What kind of boredom is defended?
options: Chosen emptiness, like a fallow field
